population.note: FICTIONAL. About 262M US adults × 19.6% ≈ 51.4M current users. Ever-used is 26% ≈ 68M, so ~6.4% of adults (≈16.8M) have used a drug and are off it now. Cycling arithmetic: with ~35% one-year persistence and ~40% restarting within a year, ~45% of current users are restarters (0.45 × 19.6 ≈ 8.8 pts), and ~1.0 pt of the off-now group restarted once before stopping again. That gives (8.8 + 1.0) / 26 ≈ 38% of ever-users who have stopped and restarted at least once. Who pays for the ~51M (reconciles to the total): fills coded for diabetes, cardiac, OSA or kidney disease across all payers ~22M; commercial obesity-coded coverage ~9M; Medicare obesity coverage ~2.0M; Medicaid obesity ~2.5M; cash-pay via TrumpRx, manufacturer direct and telehealth ~12M (incl. ~2.5M on low-dose 'craving/focus' subscriptions); gray market (compounded remnants, imported Indian/Canadian generics, 'research peptide' tirzepatide and retatrutide) ~4M. The income gradient widened as employer obesity coverage retreated; the bottom third relies on diabetes codes and Medicaid. The 65+ band rose to 16% (~9.6M of ~60M), covered by Medicare for diabetes (~5.5M) and obesity (~2.0M), plus cash (~2.1M). Under-18 use is ~1% overall, mostly ages 12–17 with obesity plus off-label 8–11 under specialists; upper-income children are still about 1.5× as likely to be prescribed. The off-drug population has three faces. First, the ~17M who stopped, mostly over cost or GI effects, many of them regaining. Second, the never-able: uninsured or employer-dropped people with obesity, concentrated in the bottom third and the South. Third, the never-willing, who are now the ones asked to explain themselves.

access.public_coverage: Medicare: obesity coverage carried on past the Bridge pilot's Dec 2027 end, on the terms of the Nov 2025 manufacturer agreement. Medicare pays ~$245/month, beneficiary copay ~$50, BMI/comorbidity criteria apply. About 2.0M beneficiaries are covered for obesity: 2.0M × $245 × 12 ≈ $5.9B/year gross. The CBO scored ≥$35B over 2026–2034 (~$3.9B/year average), so spending runs roughly 50% above the score's annual pace. Medicaid pays the same $245 rate in states that opted in: ~2.5M obesity-coded users × $245 × 12 ≈ $7.4B/year, shared between federal and state budgets. Diabetes, cardiovascular, OSA and CKD indications are covered as before across all public programmes.
access.generic_rest_of_world: India: 50+ generic semaglutide brands at ~$8–48/month; bulk API exports have been licence-controlled since the 2027 US tariffs. Canada: generics at ~CAD 88–120/month; Health Canada's bulk-export prohibition limits cross-border flow to personal quantities. Brazil and China (patent lapsed 2026) produce at scale. Generic semaglutide is available in ~160 countries. US exclusivity still runs to ~2031–32.
access.note: FICTIONAL. Prices stalled. The TrumpRx/direct cash step-down to $245 for injectables never arrived: Lilly and Novo held cash injectable prices at $299–349 after the 2027 Section 232 pharmaceutical tariffs and a supply crunch on oral starter doses. Oral entry doses (Wegovy pill, Foundayo) are still $149–150; oral maintenance doses are $249–299. List prices are unchanged (Wegovy $1,349). Employer coverage for weight management fell from 60% to 44% (Business Group on Health, 2027–28). Most remaining plans require a diabetes, cardiac, OSA or CKD code, or BMI ≥40. The result is a two-tier system where the diagnosis code, not the body, decides who pays. The gray market grew from 'contained' to 'significant' (~4M users, ~8% of all users). The 503B exclusion was finalised, but Chinese-origin 'research peptide' vials of tirzepatide and unapproved retatrutide, sold via Telegram and gym networks, plus imported Indian generics, fill the gap. Orals are ~35% of new starts; weekly injectables remain the majority among continuing users.

on_market_classes: GIP/GLP-1 dual agonist, weekly injectable (tirzepatide: Zepbound/Mounjaro)
GLP-1 agonist, daily oral peptide (Wegovy pill, 25 mg; Rybelsus)
GLP-1 agonist, daily injectable (liraglutide: Saxenda, incl. generics)
indications_beyond_weight_and_diabetes: alcohol use disorder in adults with overweight or obesity (semaglutide/Wegovy, FDA Jun 2028; ASAM/APA guideline-endorsed Oct 2027)
mainstream_offlabel_uses: 'quiet mind' / craving-and-focus low-dose regimens (Foundayo and Wegovy pill entry doses) sold by telehealth subscriptions to people without obesity, marketed around food noise, scrolling, shopping and 'mental noise'; no mood indication exists
alcohol reduction in people without obesity, extrapolated from the AUD label
nicotine and vaping cessation (observational data and small RCTs, no approval)
pediatric under-12 use under specialist care, now with growth monitoring after the 2028 signal
gray-market retatrutide for maximal loss, unapproved
drugs.pipeline_note: No new class reached the US market in 2026–28. CagriSema: FDA complete response letter (Dec 2026) requested additional data after REDEFINE-4; Novo resubmitted mid-2028, decision due 2029. Retatrutide: BLA filed Q1 2027; FDA extended the review after a major amendment covering the dysesthesia and discontinuation data; decision expected H1 2029. It is nonetheless the best-selling gray-market peptide. Amycretin and survodutide are in phase 3 (survodutide filing expected 2029). MariTide (monthly) is in phase 3, not filed. Bimagrumab-type muscle adjuncts are in phase 2/3. The 'mood and motivation' driver is realised through off-label telehealth marketing of existing low-dose orals, not an FDA indication; Novo has a phase 2 trial of oral semaglutide in binge-eating and compulsive behaviours. Market growth slowed because US prices stalled and tariffs bit: ~$110B global incretin revenue in 2028.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Most common class effect; concentrated at initiation and dose escalation; leading cause of discontinuation and the main reason cyclers stop.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled; Ozempic 'not recommended in severe gastroparesis'.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Long-term RCTs still have not confirmed causation; absolute risk is low; gray-market dosing errors muddy surveillance.
~25–30% of weight lost is lean mass. Bone-density and fracture concerns are concentrated among users aged 65+, whose numbers grew to ~9.6M.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: No regulatory action; geriatric societies recommend resistance training and protein counselling; adjunct drugs are still in trials.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Cohort studies still conflict; absolute risk is very low.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: EMA 'very rare' label stands; no US class label.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No causal association found by EMA, MHRA or systematic reviews.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Warning removed from US labels (Jan 2026); not restored.

safety_ledger.effect: Reward blunting / emotional flattening ('Ozempic personality', anhedonia)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: A 2027 prospective survey cohort (n≈9,000) found ~10% of users report clinically meaningful loss of pleasure or motivation. The effect is dose-related and largely reversible on dose reduction. It is the same effect telehealth firms now sell as 'quiet'.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Nothing on labels. FDA sent warning letters to three telehealth firms for implied mood or focus claims (2028); manufacturers decline to promote the effect.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Trial and real-world figures have converged on roughly half to two-thirds of lost weight regained within a year; cycling is now the modal pattern.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None; underpins the chronic-therapy framing and employers' cost objections.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Further observational reports of iron, B12 and vitamin D deficiency with sustained low intake.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None; the supplement industry markets 'GLP-1 companion' multivitamins.

safety_ledger.effect: Long-horizon effects beyond ~5 years of continuous use; effects of repeated on/off cycling
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Semaglutide now has ~6 years of RCT follow-up; the effects of cycling are still unstudied even though 38% of ever-users cycle.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Postmarketing requirements on new approvals; no cycling study mandated.

safety_ledger.effect: Compounded / counterfeit / research-peptide harms (dosing errors, contamination, unapproved molecules)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Compounded-product reports fell after the 503B exclusion, but ER visits linked to gray-market tirzepatide and retatrutide vials rose; ~4M users are on gray-market product.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: 503B exclusion finalised; CBP seizes peptide shipments; warning letters continue at a lower cadence.

safety_ledger.effect: Pediatric developmental signal: slowed height velocity and restrictive-eating diagnoses in children who started young
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: An Apr 2028 multi-network pediatric cohort (~14,000 treated) found that children starting before age 14 grew ~1 cm/year less over two years than matched controls. They also had more delayed-puberty codes and roughly double the rate of new ARFID/restrictive-eating diagnoses (absolute rates low, ~1–2%). Confounding by obesity severity and by weight loss itself is unresolved.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA requested label language on growth monitoring and a postmarketing study; AAP interim guidance urges growth and pubertal monitoring and caution under age 12; EMA PRAC review opened.

food_and_beverage.state: GLP-1 households are now ~30% of US households. Snacks, confectionery and sugary drinks are in sustained low-single-digit volume decline, with mergers and SKU culls (two mid-size snack makers sold to private equity). Protein, fibre, 'mini' formats and high-intensity flavours (sour, spicy) are the growth lines. Test kitchens in Columbus, Ohio now design for a shopper who eats less but pays more per bite.

alcohol.state: Heavy-drinker attrition deepened with the AUD label and guideline endorsement. US spirits volume is down mid-single digits over two years; Brown-Forman and other Kentucky distillers cut shifts and barrel commitments. Non-alcoholic and 'functional' drinks absorb some drinking occasions but not the revenue.

restaurants.state: Traffic is roughly flat. Smaller-plate and 'half portion' menus are standard in casual dining; buffets and all-you-can-eat concepts are closing locations; fine dining leans on tasting menus with tiny courses.

apparel.state: Plus-size specialists keep shrinking, with store closures at Torrid and DXL. Mainstream retailers have finished the resizing wave, so the re-buying bump has faded and size curves have shifted down.

fitness.state: Strength-training studios and 'GLP-1 companion' memberships are growing. In some cities gyms double as informal gray-market peptide channels, a reputational problem for the chains.

insurance.state: Employer obesity coverage fell from 60% to 44%, and the remaining plans gate on diabetes or cardiac codes. Pressure on diagnosis coding ('find the prediabetes') is a known phenomenon. Pharmacy trend is still high single digits. Public programmes are absorbing older users at costs above their budget scores.

pharma.state: The duopoly is intact. Lilly is positioned as the US 'national champion' with domestic plants; Novo pays tariff-driven costs while expanding North Carolina fill-finish. US prices have stalled while ex-US prices collapse, and revenue growth is slower than 2026 forecasts.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: Being on it is unremarkable; a larger body now reads as uninsured, unwilling, or between cycles. Being off it is what people explain at dinner: cost, side effects, pregnancy, principle.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: The two-tier system is visible. Thinness tracks diagnosis codes and employer generosity, and the bottom income third uses at half the rate of the top. In the rural South, gray-market vials are how many people get it. Abroad, generic semaglutide makes thinness cheap; in the US it remains a $299–349 monthly line item.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: Half-portions, shared plates and tasting-sized courses are normal; holiday meals are shorter; the office birthday cake often goes uneaten. Food is increasingly chosen for intensity rather than volume.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: Dating profiles in big metros routinely state 'on Zep' or 'off it' as neutral facts. Some couples coordinate cycling around trips or trying to conceive. Complaints of lowered libido are common enough to be a sitcom joke.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: Appetite is treated as noise to be tuned. Strong desire for food, drink, shopping or scrolling is increasingly framed as a dial setting rather than part of the self.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: ~10% of users report meaningful loss of pleasure or motivation (2027 cohort). A further minority, including ~2.5M low-dose subscribers, seek the quieting deliberately. Whether it counts as a side effect or a product depends on who is describing it.
interior_life.framing: Feature: telehealth firms sell 'quiet', 'freedom from craving' and 'calm focus' with low-dose orals. Clinicians still call the unwanted version a side effect, and the AUD label makes it a treatment. All three framings coexist.
interior_life.effect_on_work: Quiet-mind subscriptions cluster in tech, finance and law in Austin, San Francisco and New York, marketed as an alternative to stimulants and evening drinking. Managers informally notice calmer, less impulsive staff. Sales and hospitality workers more often report losing their edge, and stop. No employer programme encourages it.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: Musicians and comics openly debate 'flat' work, and a strand of 2028 indie music is pointedly sparse. Experiences sold as 'feel something' are growing: cold plunges, extreme sour food, loud immersive shows. Gambling and sports-betting firms see softer engagement among on-drug customers.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: Lowered desire and emotional muting are common complaints. Some couples treat cycling off as 'getting each other back', and therapists report more sessions about a partner who 'got quiet'.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: No measured effect on turnout or partisanship. The live political issue is price: the US-versus-India gap and the tariffs are 2028 campaign material, and 'why does Canada get it for $90' is a bipartisan applause line.

state.regulatory_posture: Unchanged: pro-access approvals and a crackdown on compounders and on telehealth mood claims. Reviews of next-generation drugs have been slower (CagriSema CRL, retatrutide review extended).
state.subsidy_or_mandate: No new action. Medicare and Medicaid obesity coverage continue at the 2025-deal rate (~$245, ~$50 copay). No mandate, and no extension of coverage to people whose employers dropped it.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: Coverage is conditioned on BMI, comorbidity codes and prior authorisation; there is no adherence monitoring. Telehealth subscriptions collect craving and mood self-tracking data under ordinary consumer privacy rules.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: Section 232 tariffs (2027) hit branded pharmaceutical imports from firms without US production, and Indian API. Lilly is cast as the national champion while Novo shifts fill-finish to North Carolina. India licenses bulk API exports, Health Canada bans bulk export of generic semaglutide, and CBP seizes Chinese peptide shipments.

events.event: Section 232 pharmaceutical tariffs take effect on branded imports from firms without US production and on Indian active ingredients. Lilly touts its Indiana and North Carolina plants, Novo accelerates US fill-finish, India moves to license bulk semaglutide API exports, and Health Canada bans bulk export of generic semaglutide.

Lilly and Novo halt the planned TrumpRx step-down to $245, holding cash prices for injectables at $299–349 and citing tariff costs and oral starter-dose shortages; the 503B compounding exclusion is finalised.
Business Group on Health survey: the share of large employers covering weight-loss drugs falls to 44%, and most remaining plans now require a diabetes, cardiac, sleep-apnea or kidney diagnosis.

Pediatric cohort study links GLP-1 starts before age 14 to slower height growth and more restrictive-eating diagnoses; the FDA asks for label language on growth monitoring and the AAP issues interim guidance.

FDA approves Wegovy for alcohol use disorder in adults with overweight or obesity, following ASAM/APA guideline endorsement in October 2027. Telehealth 'quiet mind' subscriptions using low-dose orals pass an estimated 2.5 million members and draw FDA warning letters over implied mood claims.

Gallup: 19.6% of US adults are now on a GLP-1 and 26% have ever used one. A majority of respondents know someone currently taking one, and among adults with obesity, non-users now outnumber users only in the bottom income third.

open_tensions: Prices stalled at home and collapsed abroad, with tariffs and export controls in between. The US–India–Canada gap is now an electoral issue with no policy attached, and a growing gray market is filling it.
The diagnosis code, not the body, decides who pays. Employers have retreated to diabetes and cardiac codes, while coding pressure, cycling and Medicare's overrun of the CBO score keep accumulating.
Reward quieting is simultaneously an FDA-approved treatment (AUD), a marketed lifestyle product and a reported harm, and it is regulated only by warning letters.
Children who started young show a growth and eating-disorder signal that no one's data can yet separate from confounding, while pediatric prescribing keeps rising in affluent families.
still_true: Wegovy list price remains $1,349/month, and almost nobody pays it.
No FDA-approved generic semaglutide or tirzepatide exists in the US; exclusivity still runs to roughly 2031–32.
Medicare pays ~$245/month with a ~$50 beneficiary copay for eligible obesity coverage, as set in the November 2025 deal.
Oral initial doses (Wegovy pill, Foundayo) remain priced at $149–150 per month.
The FDA's January 2026 removal of the suicidal-ideation warning stands, and there is still no US class label for NAION.

prose.headline: One in Five and Holding: America Got Quiet, But Only If It Has the Right Diagnosis Code
prose.world_in_600_words:
By the end of 2028 roughly one American adult in five is taking an incretin drug, and the remarkable thing is how unremarkable it has become. In Columbus, Ohio, where food companies run test kitchens, the target shopper eats half a sandwich and pays more for it. In Louisville, distillers have cut shifts. At suburban dinner tables, the person who has to explain themselves is the one not taking anything: they can't afford it, the nausea was too much, they're trying to get pregnant, they just don't want to.

Prices were supposed to keep falling and didn't. The 2025 deals promised a cash path down to $245 a month. Then the 2027 pharmaceutical tariffs arrived, oral starter doses ran short, and Lilly and Novo held cash injectables at $299 to $349. Wegovy's list price is still $1,349, a number that now exists mainly for lawsuits. The entry-dose pills stay at $149, and that one fact shapes a whole market. Meanwhile in India, generic semaglutide costs less than a streaming subscription, and in Canada about ninety dollars. Ottawa has banned bulk exports, New Delhi licenses its ingredient shipments, and Lilly, with its Indiana plants, gets talked about as a national champion. A drug that used to be an endocrine story is now a trade story.

Employers kept leaving. Only 44 percent of large employers still cover weight loss, and most of those want a diabetes, heart, sleep-apnea or kidney diagnosis first. The result is two tiers that run on paperwork. A woman with a prediabetes code is covered. Her husband, the same weight but without the code, pays cash or stops. The bottom income third uses these drugs at half the rate of the top. Where the formal market is too expensive, the gray market has grown: research-peptide vials from Chinese suppliers, unapproved retatrutide passed around gyms, generics carried back over the northern border. Medicare kept the $245 terms after its bridge pilot ended, and its obesity spending is running about half again above the budget office's yearly pace.

No new drug class arrived. CagriSema got a complete response letter. Retatrutide's review was extended into 2029, which hasn't stopped it from becoming the most-wanted vial on Telegram. What did arrive was a new idea of what the old drugs are for. In June the FDA approved Wegovy for alcohol use disorder in people with overweight or obesity, after the addiction psychiatrists endorsed it. In the same months, telehealth companies built subscription brands around low-dose orals for people with no weight to lose. They sell quiet: less food noise, less scrolling, less impulse buying, a calmer head at 4 p.m. Roughly two and a half million people pay for it. The FDA sends warning letters when the ads promise mood, so the ads promise freedom from craving instead.

The flattening that people complained about in 2026 now has a number, about one user in ten, and two kinds of customer. Some want it gone and lower their dose. Others are paying for it. Programmers in Austin talk about it the way an earlier generation talked about quitting drinking. Comics complain that rooms laugh less. Couples cycle off for anniversaries.

Then there are the children. In April a large pediatric study found that kids who started before fourteen grew about a centimetre a year less than matched peers and were diagnosed more often with restrictive eating. The absolute numbers are small and the confounding is serious. Pediatricians have started measuring height more carefully. Affluent families, who are most likely to have a child on the drug, are reading the study closely and, mostly, not stopping.

Nothing has collapsed. Life just feels more muted, and it still costs a lot of money.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Dana Ruiz pulls into the dental office lot in Mesa at 7:40 and finishes half a protein bar in the car. The other half goes back in the cup holder, where yesterday's half already is.

Her Mounjaro costs twenty-five dollars because her chart says prediabetes. Her husband Ray's chart doesn't, so he came off it in March when the plan changed. He's put back fourteen pounds and says he doesn't mind. At the barbecue his brother asked him why, as if Ray had dropped out of something.

At lunch Kelsey from the front desk taps her phone, and an app called Still asks how loud her cravings are today, one to five. She pays $149 for the little pill and says it got her off her phone. She looks rested. She also looks a little like the hold music.

At four Dana leaves early to take Mateo, fourteen, to the pediatrician. The Wegovy pens are $349 a month and come off the TrumpRx card, which is the vacation now. The nurse has him stand against the wall twice and writes the number down twice. Dr. Okafor brings up the April study in a level voice, says the words growth velocity, and says they'll check again in three months.

In the car Mateo asks if he's going to be short. Dana says his grandfather was five-six and happy. He puts his earbuds in.

At dinner Ray eats seconds. Dana watches him, and she can't tell if what she feels is envy, or if she's feeling much of anything.
